titleTag: When Do US Visa Appointment Slots Actually Open?
h1: When Do US Visa Appointment Slots Actually Open? What the Missions Themselves Publish
deck: There is no global release time, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. Release is set post by post, some missions publish their own schedule in writing, and the rest follow patterns you can work with once you know what you are looking at.
metaDescription: There is no single time US visa slots open. Release is set per mission, some publish their window in writing, and here is what actually works for the rest.

coverSpec.title: US visa appointment slots come from two different supplies: scheduled bulk releases and continuous cancellations
coverSpec.desc: Appointment release is set mission by mission. Mission UAE publishes a Friday window of 7:30 to 11:30. The US Embassy in the Dominican Republic publishes Wednesdays at 8 a.m. Most posts publish nothing, and at those the real supply is cancellations returning to the pool at no fixed hour. Excessive refreshing triggers temporary account restrictions of roughly 24 to 72 hours.

faq.q: What time do US visa appointment slots open?
faq.a: There is no single time, and any article that gives you one is describing one country at best. Release is configured post by post. A few missions publish their window: Mission UAE states that nonimmigrant interview appointments are released every Friday morning between 7:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m., and the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic states that new B-1/B-2 appointments open every Wednesday at 8 a.m. Most posts publish nothing at all.

faq.q: Is there a secret time when slots appear, like midnight?
faq.a: No. The midnight theory is the most persistent myth in this subject and it survives because portals do housekeeping around date boundaries, which makes screens change without any new appointments existing. Where a real schedule is known it is a working-hours schedule at the post, not the middle of the night. Losing sleep over it costs you and buys nothing.

faq.q: Where do slots actually come from if my post does not publish a schedule?
faq.a: From two different supplies. Bulk releases are when the post loads a new block of dates, which is scheduled but usually unannounced. Cancellations are individual appointments returning to the pool when somebody else moves or drops theirs, and those appear continuously at no fixed hour. At a post with a long queue, cancellations are the supply you are realistically competing for.

faq.q: How often should I check for an earlier US visa appointment?
faq.a: Often enough to catch a cancellation, rarely enough to avoid being restricted. A few deliberate checks a day, spread out, is a sustainable rhythm. The State Department's own wait times guidance tells applicants to check back frequently and move to an earlier slot if one appears, so the method is officially endorsed. Continuous automated-speed refreshing is not, and it will get your account temporarily limited.

faq.q: Can refreshing too much get me blocked?
faq.a: It can get you temporarily restricted, typically for something in the region of 24 to 72 hours. It usually shows up as pages that stop loading, sessions that end immediately, or a calendar returning nothing where it previously returned something. It clears on its own. Switching browser, device or network to keep going repeats the behaviour that caused it, so the fix is to stop for a day.

faq.q: Does the portal show slot times in my time zone or the consulate's?
faq.a: Appointment times are the consulate's local times, because that is when you have to be standing at the door. If you are checking from another country, or your post is in a different time zone from your city, work in the post's local time for everything, including any published release window. This trips up applicants in large countries more than anyone else.

faq.q: Are more slots released after holidays?
faq.a: Often, yes, and it is one of the few patterns that holds across posts. Consular sections do not process interviews on US or local holidays, so a closure compresses work and the days after it tend to see movement, including cancellations from people whose plans changed over the break. Published release windows also skip holidays, which means the following release can be larger than usual.
